newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia hosts China, India leaders, mulls changes.
newsitem.headline: Russia hosts China, India leaders, mulls changes.

text.p: Russia turned its attention to eastern neighbours on Tuesday, days after a Russian-U.S. summit that highlighted stark differences with the West over European security.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen were scheduled for talks with Russian leaders who face social conflict at home to match their foreign policy woes.
Both countries have, at different times, enjoyed close links with the Kremlin.
India was long the leading supporter of Soviet foreign policy in the non-aligned movement. Beijing, a close ally of Moscow in the 1950s, subsequently became its arch ideological foe.
Russia, facing economic crisis at home and political differences with the West in its transition to capitalism, needs to reinvigorate commercial and political ties with both regional giants.

Deve Gowda is expected to meet President Boris Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Tuesday to discuss bilateral economic relations, with military cooperation high on the agenda. India has in the past been a good market for Russia's increasingly assertive arms industry.
Qian, who meets Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Tuesday, is paving the way for a visit next month by President Ziang Zemin.

But Qian's trip started out awkwardly. He had to wait 20 minutes in Moscow's gloomy Sheremetyevo airport for Russia's official welcoming party to arrive. Foreign Ministry officials complained that the airport had misinformed them about Qian's arrival time.

The leaders from the world's most populous countries are visiting Moscow just days after Yeltsin's Helsinki summit with Clinton, at which the two leaders "agreed to disagree" over NATO plans to invite former Soviet bloc states to join the Western defence alliance.
After a honeymoon following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia's relations with the United States have lost some of their early glow, partially over NATO expansion.

As Russia's leaders looked eastward in foreign policy, they also signaled that further domestic moves are afoot ahead of a day-long strike on Thursday which trade union leaders say will attract millions of protesters nationwide.
The unions are calling for payment of wages, which they say are five months late on average, as well as the government's resignation.
Yeltsin has preempted some of the demands by starting a dramatic government reshuffle earlier this month which made young reformers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov deputy prime ministers.

On Monday, Prime Minister Chernomyrdin admitted federal and local authorities, and especially employers, had done "far from everything" to ensure workers received wages on time and promised the government would take "the most drastic measures" to sort out delays.

Russian Public Television said on Monday night that Chernomyrdin, Chubais and Nemtsov were expected to hold a joint press conference in the coming days, signaling a possible announcement on the issue.
Chernomyrdin also said on Monday the bulk of the changes in the cabinet would be completed this week.
But the government's latest moves did not win over voters in three Russian regions that went to the polls on Sunday.
Communist Vasily Starodubtsev, a leader of the 1991 hardline coup against Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev, won the governorship seat in Tula, south of Moscow.
Another communist won a governorship in the Amur region bordering China and a nationalist won a seat in the lower house of parliament in the southern region of Voronezh.
